Hey, I'm glad you're here — thanks for stopping by!

I'm a computational scientist at [The Jackson Laboratory](https://www.jax.org/people/selcan-aydin) in Bar Harbor, Maine,
working in the [Munger Lab](https://www.jax.org/research-and-faculty/research-labs/the-munger-lab).
My research sits at the intersection of **quantitative genetics**, **systems biology**, and **developmental biology**,
with a focus on how genetic variation shapes gene regulation and cell fate decisions in mice.

Get in touch by [sending me an email](mailto:selcan.aydin@jax.org)!

---

## About me

**Computational biologist with interdisciplinary roots — from mathematical modeling of cell signaling to systems genetics of development.**

I grew up in Istanbul, Turkey, and my scientific journey has taken me from modeling biochemical networks in Heidelberg,
to mapping the genetics of stress responses in yeast at Duke, to studying how genetic variation reshapes gene regulatory networks in mouse stem cells and their differentiated progeny.

Early in my career I realized that I thrive on interdisciplinary questions. My master's at Heidelberg introduced me to
mathematical modeling of cellular signaling, and my PhD at Duke extended this curiosity to genetic variation — asking
how differences in DNA sequence alter the way cells respond to environmental signals. Along the way I picked up a broad
toolkit: high-throughput phenotyping, fluorescence and luminescence microscopy, quantitative genetics methods, and
computational skills for handling large sequencing datasets. That training planted the seeds of my career as a
computational geneticist.

- Ph.D. in Biology · Duke University · 2017
- M.Sc. in Systems Biology · Universität Heidelberg · 2010
- B.Sc. in Biological Sciences & Bioengineering · Sabancı University · 2009

### Research at JAX

At JAX I use [Diversity Outbred (DO) mice](https://www.jax.org/strain/009376) as a resource for systems genetics,
mapping how genetic variation shapes gene regulation across multiple molecular layers and cell states. This work
traced a causal path from a single regulatory variant near *Lifr* through a cascade of molecular changes to
pluripotency maintenance
([Skelly, Czechanski, Byers, **Aydin** et al., *Cell Stem Cell*, 2020](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.stem.2020.07.005);
[Ortmann, Brown, Czechanski, **Aydin** et al., *Cell Stem Cell*, 2020](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.stem.2020.07.019)),
and showed that jointly integrating chromatin, transcript, and protein data uncovers loci invisible to single-omics
approaches
([**Aydin** et al., *Cell Genomics*, 2023](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xgen.2023.100283)).
Expanding to neural progenitor cells revealed both conserved and cell-state-specific eQTL, and demonstrated that
genetic effects established in ESCs can propagate to shape transcriptional variation in downstream differentiated cells
([**Aydin** et al., *G3*, 2025](https://doi.org/10.1093/g3journal/jkaf099);
[**Aydin** et al., preprint, 2025](https://doi.org/10.1101/2025.01.24.634514)).
We also released [QTLretrievR](https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.02.16.706200) to make molecular QTL mapping more
accessible to the community.

I'm currently applying these approaches to single-cell RNA-seq data and extending our systems genetics framework to
new biological contexts, including the developing palate. One thing that has remained constant across all of this work
is a genuine love of learning — both picking up new computational methods as the field evolves, and deepening my
understanding of the biology along the way.

### Teaching, mentoring & outreach

I am passionate about lowering barriers to computational biology for life scientists — especially skills that people
find intimidating, like statistics, coding, or working with large datasets. Because most of my own computational skills
were self-taught, I know firsthand the value of accessible, well-scaffolded training. I am a certified
[Posit (RStudio) Tidyverse Instructor](https://education.rstudio.com/trainers/people/aydin+selcan/) and a certified
Software Carpentry instructor, and I have been teaching workshops both within JAX and across the broader community.

Beyond the classroom, I am committed to making science a more equitable and welcoming place. I served on the
**Accessibility Subcommittee** of the
[GSA Early Career Scientist Committees](https://genestogenomes.org/early-career-leadership-spotlight-selcan-aydin/),
working to identify barriers faced by scientists with disabilities and develop resources to make research, labs, and
conferences more accessible. I have also been active in supporting foreign researchers navigating visa and immigration
challenges — an issue close to my own experience as an international scientist — and in raising awareness around
mental health in academia.

Outside of work I enjoy hiking, gardening, and spending time with my family and our dog Darwin. 🌿
